---
title: "Structs, Enums, and Exhaustive Pattern Matching"
description: "One key Rust idea, one tiny executable example, the reason it works, and a precise pitfall."
---

## The question

**How do you model a payment that can be either cash or a card with a fee?**

An enum represents **one of several valid cases**; the compiler checks that `match` handles them all. A struct groups fields that exist together.

## The core rule

Make invalid combinations difficult to represent.

## One complete example

Paste these lines into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`, or [use the tested Rust examples project](examples/index.qmd).

~~~rust
enum Payment { Cash, Card(u32) }
fn fee(p: Payment) -> u32 {
    match p {
        Payment::Cash => 0,
        Payment::Card(amount) => amount / 100,
    }
}
fn main() {
    println!("{}", fee(Payment::Card(500))); // 5
}
~~~

**Walk through it:** `Payment::Card(500)` carries an amount of 500 and selects the Card match arm. Dividing by 100 returns 5; `Cash` returns 0. Adding a new enum variant forces you to revisit non-exhaustive matches.

## Common misunderstanding

The data-carrying `Card(u32)` is a tuple-like enum variant. If both cash and card should store different data, use variants with appropriate fields instead of many optional fields in one struct.

## Remember it in one sentence

Make invalid combinations difficult to represent.

**Official reference:** [The Rust Programming Language / Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch06-02-match.html).
